title: Health Investment Framework: G20 Common Language Guide | World Economic Forum
gist: Health has never been organized as an asset class: DFIs share only three headcount/compliance health indicators and neither the EU taxonomy nor the G20 sustainable finance work covers health, so investors cannot underwrite it. Drawing on the 2016 G20 green-finance precedent, the article proposes a voluntary four-layer Health Investment Framework and asks the G20 to adopt a common health-investment language under the UK's 2027 presidency.

themes.theme: Health is not yet an asset class

insights.claim: Twenty-eight development finance institutions have agreed on 30 common indicators for ICT investment but only three for health (patients served, facilities accredited, number of accreditations), none of which measure health outcomes.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: DFI health impact reporting measures headcount and compliance, not outcomes, so 'health impact' claims in DFI-backed deals are hard to verify or compare.
insights.quote: For health, they have agreed on just three: patients served, facilities accredited and number of accreditations.
insights.locator: There is an asymmetry at play

insights.claim: Health has never been organized as an asset class: development banks each apply their own health lending criteria and other investors have no common reference point.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Absence of a shared definition is the structural barrier to scaled institutional capital in health, not lack of returns.
insights.quote: This asymmetry shows that health has never been organized as an asset class.

insights.claim: Neither the EU taxonomy for sustainable activities nor the G20 sustainable finance workstream includes health, whereas green finance has had market-built definitions since 2013 and an official EU classification since 2020.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Health-labelled sustainable products lack regulatory classification, leaving them exposed to inconsistency and 'health-washing' risk versus green assets.

insights.claim: Health projects sit inside social and sustainability bonds where each issuer decides what counts as a health investment, so allocators cannot compare two health assets in one portfolio.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Watch for standardised health-use-of-proceeds criteria; until then, health allocations within social bond portfolios are not comparable.
insights.quote: it is a tag with no measure of performance behind it
insights.locator: Rather, health is hard to underwrite

insights.claim: In 2022 health spending as a share of GDP fell in 33 of 38 OECD countries and in 18 G20 members, even as ageing populations and chronic disease raised demand on health systems.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Fiscal pressure is squeezing public health budgets against rising demand, widening the gap private capital could fill.
insights.locator: Finance ministers are used to requests

insights.claim: Requests for more health money are more likely to be refused when budgets are tight, and more money does not always buy better health: some G20 economies spend several times more per person than peers yet have shorter life expectancy.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Policy momentum favours efficiency and outcome-based spending over headline budget increases; outcome-linked models gain relevance.
insights.quote: Nor does more money always buy better health.
insights.locator: More money is not the answer

insights.claim: The OECD estimates healthier populations and less wasteful spending, supported by digital transformation, could hold health spending at 10.6% of GDP by 2040 versus 11.8% without major policy change, a 1.2 percentage-point gap.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A 1.2pp-of-GDP saving gives finance ministries a fiscal case for prevention and digital health tools.
insights.quote: For finance ministries, that 1.2 percentage points of GDP is a clear argument for spending more wisely.
insights.locator: More money is not the answer

insights.claim: Every $1 invested in improving population health is estimated to generate $2 to $4 in economic benefit, so returns are not what keeps health marginal in sustainable finance; the problem is that health is hard to underwrite.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: The investability gap is a measurement/definition problem, implying upside once standards arrive rather than a weak return profile.

insights.claim: In 2016 under China's presidency the G20 set up a Green Finance Study Group co-chaired with the UK, which flagged unclear definitions as a barrier; the G20 gave the issue official standing and standard setters did the rest.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Precedent suggests G20 endorsement can catalyse standard-setting and a new labelled market, as happened for green bonds.
insights.quote: By convening the work, the G20 gave the issue official standing; standard setters did the rest.
insights.locator: The G20 has done this before

insights.claim: Health finance today is where green finance was in 2016: market tools such as ICMA's health category and the SASB Health Care standards exist, but there is no shared definition of a health investment.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: If the analogy holds, a health-labelled market could follow a green-bond-like growth path once definitions standardise.
insights.quote: Health today is where green finance was in 2016
insights.locator: Health today is where green finance

insights.claim: The G20 & G7 Health and Development Partnership has built a voluntary Health Investment Framework with a steering committee including the EIB, EBRD, Council of Europe Development Bank, World Economic Forum, OECD, WHO, Milken Institute, PIMCO and UNICEF.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
entities: G20 & G7 Health and Development Partnership
insights.so_what: Involvement of DFIs and a major asset manager (PIMCO) raises odds the framework becomes a market reference.
insights.locator: A framework built from what already exists

insights.claim: The Health Investment Framework tests investments through four layers: qualifying questions, six principles (access, outcomes, system resilience, health workforce, environmental integrity, governance), thresholds and guardrails, and a final label of health-aligned, health-improving or not eligible.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A tiered label could become the basis for health-themed funds, bonds and incentive eligibility; track its adoption.
insights.quote: finally it applies a clear label of health-aligned, health-improving or not eligible
insights.locator: It tests an investment through four layers

insights.claim: The framework lets development banks crowd private co-investment into government projects, lets institutional investors label and compare health investments made outside development banks, and lets governments see what private capital in their hospitals and clinics pays for.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Blended-finance health deals alongside DFIs are the likely first use case for private investors.

insights.claim: The framework is built from existing standards (System of Health Accounts, EU taxonomy, IFRS S1, ICMA bond principles), runs on existing disclosures rather than a new reporting regime, and excludes investments that undermine referral pathways or widen access gaps.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Low incremental reporting burden improves adoption odds; exclusions signal some private health models may be screened out.
insights.quote: Nor is it a new reporting regime: it runs on disclosures institutions already make.

insights.claim: The framework's backers say it is not a request for funding and does not promote privatization, because private capital already flows into health systems unclassified.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Positioning as classification, not privatization, aims to defuse political opposition that could stall adoption.
insights.quote: private capital already flows into health systems, unclassified
insights.locator: The framework is not a request for funding

insights.claim: Consultations held alongside the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok produced four G20 asks: the Sustainable Finance Working Group should adopt a common health-investment language under the UK (2027) and South Korean (2028) presidencies; DFIs should extend health indicators beyond headcounts; one sovereign or development bank should pilot the framework on a real transaction; and finance ministries should attach existing incentives to classified investments.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Watch for a pilot sovereign/DFI health-labelled transaction and G20 SFWG agenda items in 2027-2028 as catalysts.
insights.locator: Their answers shaped four asks of the G20

insights.claim: Without finance ministries attaching existing incentives to investments it classifies, the Health Investment Framework risks becoming another label with no economic effect.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Economic value of a health label depends on incentives (tax, capital, procurement) being attached; monitor policy follow-through.
insights.quote: without that, it becomes another label with no economic effect

insights.claim: 2027 is the window because the UK holds the G20 Presidency and the UN convenes its High-Level Meeting on Universal Health Coverage, with G20 finance-track progress feeding directly into it.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Timeline for any official health-investment taxonomy centres on 2027; positioning ahead of it could matter for health-infrastructure investors.
